There are different algorithms to compressions and they have different advantages. Some are fast(i.e. GZ, LZ4) and some have better compression rate(i.e. BZip2). Tar is an archive without compression. What's best depends on what it's used for.

Zip is probably the most universal. I think any computer can open a zip file without special software. That's good if you're uploading a file intended to reach a varied user-base.

If I think it's mostly going to be nerds who are downloading a file, I'll use .rar or .7zip because those are the ones I see most often.

I think it has to do with the:

  • origin of the compression
  • target user of the compression
  • extent of the compression
  • freeness of the compression code

The origin is going to influence which compression is used. For instance a Windows user will be quick to .zip or maybe even .rar something up with WinRAR, while a Linux user will be quick .tgz or .tbz the same file.

The target of the compression will also determine which compression is used. I am primarily a Linux user, so if I wish to share a file that is to be understood by Windows, Linux, and Mac users, I'd best pick a format understand by all 3 without much fuss; I'd go with .zip. If I was on Windows and was only going to share with another Windows computer I knew would have WinRAR readily available, then I might choose .rar.

The extent of compression doesn't (in my opinion) play a huge role in compression these days since storage is so cheap, but in the past it was a big deal. A 10 MB file shrunk down to a 7MB zip or tgz vs the same file shrunk down to 6MB with bzip or rar just doesn't seem like a big deal, so most folks are going to just .zip their file and be done with it. The folks that want that extra 1MB of compression are going to deal with installing the third party compression utilities.

And then we have to bring code religion into the situation with code freeness. Some compression algorithms are closed source, others are open. Some of the suits are not going to care if the compression algorithm code is closed source, while some beards are absolutely going to care.

I can't speak for everyone and their compressional needs, but me, I'm a situational compressor. I compress based on the situation. When it's just me in my own little world practically everything I do is .tgz. When I have to deal with the outside world I often compress with .zip.
In layman terms, higher the compression, higher the cpu power and time need to compress-decompress. Theres lighter and heavier algorithms

Compression of a file can work in many ways. But they all do essentially the same thing, find patterns and tag them as a representation of a part of the original file.

Say you own a store with a window display and you want to show passers-by the best representation of your inventory. If you could fit all of your inventory in the window that would be the most accurate. But of course you can't due to space. So you take one of each item, place it at the front and people can view it and decide to come in.

Compression algorithms do that but with patterns of bits, 1's and 0's. So if 10011001 ocurs 8 times, it will take that string of bits and according to its algorithm form a placeholder for it e.g. 10.

So 10011001 becomes 10 everywhere. The algorithm you use depends on file type as some are specialized.
